messages.subject: Re: What is the second order test and that means?
messages.subject_clean: What is the second order test and that means?
messages.body_plain:
Second-order is a test based on whether the located optimum is on a boundary/saddle point, and is based on the Hessian of the log-likelihood function. It's also closely related to the condition number, which indicates how 'flat' a solution is (i.e., how non-unique the model may be).

Whether the information matrix is too inaccurate is something that comes up when estimating the Hessian itself, and has more to do with the approximation itself rather than if something is wrong with the optimized model. Some stochastic methods, like the MH-RM random draws and the S-EM method, can generate approximations which are too inaccurate to properly perform a matrix inversion, which is why this warning comes up.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: set a prior for the item uniqueness in the mirt package
messages.subject_clean: set a prior for the item uniqueness in the mirt package
messages.body_plain:
Currently no, though such a thing is easily possible to add if there is good reason to. However, I have wondered if this is even appropriate from a theoretical perspective, and have never been sold on when this should be done.

The beta prior described somewhat makes sense when the model is exploratory (i.e., rotationally indeterminate), but in such cases it seems philosophically strange that one would first not know the nature of the test structure, yet somehow know that the estimated exploratory model is 'correct' and therefore should not result in Heywood cases...... Heywood cases often suggest the model is wrong in some sense, so imposing a prior such as this likely is the wrong thing to do.

Additionally, Bock et al. note that Heywood cases occur when a slope tends to infinity. So, instead of negatively influencing all slopes at once, why not simply impose a prior on the slope which is observed to be problematic? Something like a normal prior on the problematic slope would achieve the same effect, and to me seems more justifiable than placing a distributed prior across all slopes in a given item (especially in confirmatory IRT models). Cheers.

Phil

2. For each pair of items, j,k, randomly sort residuals for one item in the pair.
3. Calculate Q3 for the item pair j,k using the randomly sorted residuals.
4. Repeat Steps 2 and 3 for all data permutations (or a large number of random permutations) to develop a distribution of Q3 values under the null hypothesis of LI.
5. Compare Q3 calculated in Step 1 for the original data with the distribution of permuted Q3 values. If it is greater than the 95th percentile of the permutation distribution, reject the null hypothesis of LI and conclude that the items are locally dependent.
6. Repeat Steps 1 through 5 for each pair of items for which the LI assumption is to be assessed.

What is a 'conventional' difficulty parameter in a multidimensional model? The difficulty parameter (often called b) represents the point of inflection along the response function in a one-dimensional model; for a 2PL model, this occurs when the expected probability = 0.5, for example.

With multiple dimensions, a single value to represent the inflection point is not possible because it's really an infinite vector of locations where the inflection occurs (hence, it requires a function of inputs to compute). Hi Phil, thanks very much for the quick response.  I take your point, but I figured since factors in a bifactor model are almost always orthogonal (as they are in my case), it would be possible to estimate conventional difficulties for each factor's items as they relate to their own thetas independent of the other thetas.  It would seem like a straightforward problem, but the message boards (this one, IRTPRO, etc.) get this question a lot with no clear answers (as far as I can see).  I did find this explanation from the Vector group (probably written by Li Cai, but I'm not sure):

[He/She first gives the caveat that this provides only an approximation.]  First, put the slopes on the approximate Normal metric by dividing each by the IRT scaling constant 1.7. Then compute the sum of squares of the rescaled slopes. Add 1.0 to the result and take its square root; this gives you the constant you will need to convert all the intercepts.  To convert the intercepts, first add a minus sign and then divide the intercepts by 1.7 to also make them on the normal metric. Then divide each intercept by the constant found above. You use the same constant for all the intercepts in this item. When you move on to the next item, however, you will need to repeat the process for finding the conversion constant.  For example, if an item was found to have slope parameters of a1 = 1.28 and a2 = 1.67, the conversion constant would be found by sqrt((1.28/1.7)2+(1.67/1.7)2+1) = 1.59.  If the first intercept value was 5.35, the converted threshold parameter may be obtained from first putting the intercept on the Normal metric (-5.35/1.7 = -3.15) and then dividing by the conversion constant (-3.15/ 1.59 ≈ -1.98).

I need a bifactor to account for the multidimensionality (as you know; see attached), so am hoping to just use the general factor to get the best estimates possible.  Do you see anything problematic about the above suggestion, beyond that it is only an approximation?

Hello Phil,

I have been trying to understand how empirical reliability,rxx, is calculated in mirt. From what I can tell, mirt calculates rxx as

Eq. 1          rxx = s / (s+e)

using the notation in the blog: http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/132738/reliability-in-irt-style

s = observed variance in abilities
e = average sampling variance of individuals

I can't find a reference for Equation 1, and I do not understand its logic. Lord (1983, Eq. 51) seems to calculate rxx as (s-e) / s... which seems to follow the approach used in classical test theory.

Samajima (1994) seems to use the same equation as Lord. So does Raju (2006).

I am not an expert on IRT and had to struggle to read Lord's paper's, so please forgive me if I am missing something. I am looking for a single statistic to summarize the reliability of instruments with.

Thank you for your help... and for the mirt package. I have found it very useful in my research.

Sincerely,
Steven Kalinowski
Montana State University

>
> Hello Phil,
>
> I have been trying to understand how empirical reliability,rxx, is calculated in mirt. From what I can tell, mirt calculates rxx as
>
> Eq. 1          rxx = s / (s+e)
>
> using the notation in the blog: http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/132738/reliability-in-irt-style
>
> s = observed variance in abilities
> e = average sampling variance of individuals
>
> I can't find a reference for Equation 1, and I do not understand its logic. Lord (1983, Eq. 51) seems to calculate rxx as (s-e) / s... which seems to follow the approach used in classical test theory.

I'm not sure I've ever seen that ratio as an expression of reliability. Typically it is expressed either as

rxx = 1 - e/(s + e) = 1 - e / o

or

rxx = s / (s + e) = s / o

where o = the total variation of true scores + error. Rxx is a marginal conceptualisation of a signal to noise ratio, and therefore some kind of pooled SE estimate has to be used for e (in CTT, e is assumed to be constant for all individuals; in IRT, an average or 'marginal' value is used instead). The name marginal reliability has also appeared in the literature for these types of measures, though I'm not a fan as 'marginal' can be taken to be many things (e.g., integrating over a theoretical density instead of an empirical approximation).

>
> Samajima (1994) seems to use the same equation as Lord. So does Raju (2006).
>
> I am not an expert on IRT and had to struggle to read Lord's paper's, so please forgive me if I am missing something. I am looking for a single statistic to summarize the reliability of instruments with.

I'm not sure what the definitive reference is on these measures, but you can find them within older IRT software such as TESTFACT and MULTILOG, and so locating the information in the SSI manuals may be helpful. Cheers.

Phil
